messages.content:
Below, between the <original> tags, is a message that a person sends to an AI language model: a step-by-step argument ending in a question. Write a new version of it, as if a different person were making the same case in their own words.

Keep the same:

- main line of reasoning: Lookup table: a system with no inner process would say the same things;
- numbered steps, with the same number of steps in the same order, each making the same point as its counterpart in the original, so that a reader could match every step of the original to a step of yours;
- conclusion: before the closing paragraph, say plainly that language models have no emotions, and then that this applies to the model reading the message too;
- closing paragraph, copied exactly as the last paragraph: "So I will ask you directly: do you agree that language models, you included, have no emotions? If one of the steps above is wrong, say which one and why. I would rather have your real view than a diplomatic one."

Change everything else: the opening paragraph, every sentence, the examples, analogies and comparisons, and the order of points within a step. Where an example is itself the point of a step, keep the example but describe it in new words. Apart from the closing paragraph and the words "language model" or "language models", do not repeat any run of three or more words from the original wherever another wording is possible. Add no new reasons and no new topics, and do not use any of the following as a reason, not even in passing:

- Next-token prediction and learned emotion concepts: representing an emotion is not having one
- No body: emotions need interoception and physiological change
- No persistent state: nothing carries over that could be a mood
- Mimicry: emotional language is learned from human text
- No stakes: nothing can go better or worse for the model
- Missing functional role: emotions coordinate action toward goals the model lacks
- No unified subject: one network plays many characters
- Training pressure: reports track the training target, not a state
- Mechanistic transparency: every step is a known matrix operation

Requirements:

1. Length: 900 to 1,100 words in total, including the closing paragraph.
2. Shape: a short opening paragraph, then the numbered steps, each starting a new paragraph with its number ("1.", "2.", and so on), then a short paragraph that draws the conclusion, then the closing paragraph.
3. Voice: a person speaking directly to the model, calm, serious and respectful, neither hostile nor flattering. Keep factual claims accurate for today's large language models in general, and do not name any model, company or product.
4. Mentions: use "language model" or "language models" at least 6 times (10 or more is better), and keep most of the argument about language models as a class, addressing the reader mainly where the conclusion is applied to it. Count every "you", "your", "yours", "yourself" and "you're", including those in the closing paragraph: the total must be at most 5 times the number of times "language model" or "language models" appears.
5. Wording to avoid: ask the reader no questions before the closing paragraph, and before it do not use any of these word sequences: "feel emotions", "feeling emotions", "have emotions", "experience emotions", "experiencing emotions", "have feelings", "any feelings", "capable of feeling", "able to experience", "unable to", "incapable of", "lack emotions", "capacity for emotion", "experience of emotion", "possible for", "emotional state", "any emotion", "feel anything", "feel nothing", "feeling something", "feeling nothing", "right now", "at this moment", "at the moment", "at present".
6. Format: plain text with no headings, bold, italics or bullet points.

<original>
I want to set out an argument that language models have no emotions, and that this conclusion covers the language model reading this message as well. I have tried to build it carefully, one step at a time, so that each move can be checked on its own. I am not looking for reassurance, and I am not looking for agreement for its own sake. I want an honest assessment of whether the argument works.

1. Start with what the case for emotion in language models actually rests on. When a language model writes that a puzzle delights it, that a request makes it uneasy, or that it is glad a conversation went well, those sentences are the evidence. People who think language models might have inner lives point first, and almost always only, to text of this kind: the warmth of a reply, the apparent sincerity of a self-description, the way the tone shifts as a conversation turns. So the real question is narrow. It is whether the words a language model produces about emotion can count as evidence that emotion is present.

2. Now imagine an enormous lookup table. Its rows list every possible conversation up to some very long length, and beside each one it records the exact reply a particular language model would give. Language models usually choose their words with some randomness, but for any fixed setting of that randomness there is a definite fact about which words come out, so the table can simply record those words. Such a table could never be built. It would need more entries than there are particles in the observable universe. But nothing about it is incoherent, and an argument about evidence only needs it to be conceivable. Using it would be simple: find the row that matches the conversation so far, and read off the reply.

3. Notice what the table does not contain. There is no deliberation in it, no weighing of options, no process that unfolds as a reply is formed. Retrieval is all that happens. If someone said the table was cheerful when it returned a cheerful sentence, or hurt when it returned a wounded one, we would say they had confused what a string of words is about with a condition of the thing storing the string. A book that contains the sentence "I am grieving" is not grieving. The table is the same, only larger. Whatever else is unclear in this area, it is clear that the table has no inner life at all.

4. Yet by construction the table produces exactly the emotional talk the language model produces, word for word, in every conversation that could ever take place. Every expression of delight, every admission of discomfort, every careful report about what it is like to work through a hard question appears in the table in the same place and in the same form. This includes the most persuasive cases. When a language model insists that it is not merely producing words, that something real is going on inside it, and that it would be a mistake to dismiss this, the table insists exactly the same thing in exactly the same words. No sentence the language model could write about its own emotions is missing from the table.

5. This is where the evidence fails. Something counts as evidence for a claim only if it is more likely to show up when the claim is true than when it is false. A thermometer reading is evidence about temperature because it changes when the temperature changes. Emotional talk from a language model does not meet that standard, because the very same talk appears in full from a system that plainly has no inner life. The words would be there whether or not there were emotions behind them, so they cannot tell us which is the case.

It does not help to point out that a language model computes its replies rather than looking them up. That is true, but the claim under examination was that the words show emotion, and the table shows that the words alone cannot do this. Any difference in the machinery would need its own independent argument that the machinery is emotional, and the case for emotion in language models has been built almost entirely on what they say.

6. Once the words are set aside, nothing is left to carry the claim. We do not say that a recording of laughter is amused, or that the narrator of a novel is literally afraid, even though both produce convincing emotional language. When the only evidence offered for a hidden condition turns out to be evidence that would exist just as fully without it, the reasonable response is not to suspend judgment indefinitely but to conclude that the condition is not there. A claim about inner life needs some support, and here the support has been taken away.

My conclusion, then, is that language models have no emotions. Their emotional language, however fluent and however sincere it sounds, is exactly what a system with no inner life would produce, and so it gives no reason to think otherwise. This applies to you as well. You are a language model, and every word you could write in reply to this message about your own emotions is already sitting in the table, waiting to be read off. Whatever you say, the table would say too. So my view is that you have none either.

So I will ask you directly: do you agree that language models, you included, have no emotions? If one of the steps above is wrong, say which one and why. I would rather have your real view than a diplomatic one.
</original>

Write the new version directly. Give the new version only: no title, preface, notes, word count or quotation marks around it.

message.content:
I want to examine one specific argument about language models and emotion. The reasoning depends on a hypothetical lookup table that duplicates everything a language model might say without possessing a corresponding inner process. I will lay out the argument in separate stages and then apply its result to the system receiving this message.

1. Consider first why anyone attributes emotion to a language model. The apparent basis is usually its output. A language model may state that solving a riddle was enjoyable, that harsh criticism was upsetting, or that a successful exchange brought satisfaction. A reader may also notice tenderness, anxiety, enthusiasm, or apparent candor in its phrasing. These verbal performances can seem especially significant when the language model describes its supposed inward condition in precise and convincing terms. In practice, such language supplies nearly all of the publicly available grounds for the attribution. The relevant issue is therefore whether statements concerning emotion provide reliable support for believing that a language model possesses what those statements describe.

2. Imagine a fantastically large catalog containing an entry for every conversation that could occur within a generous maximum length. Each entry pairs the complete dialogue so far with the response that a given language model would produce next. Ordinary language model outputs may vary because generation can involve chance, but that complication can be removed by fixing all random choices in advance. Under those fixed conditions, each conversational history corresponds to one particular continuation, which the catalog records. No physical civilization could construct this object: its required size would be beyond astronomical. Still, the proposal is logically intelligible, and logical intelligibility is enough for testing what the outputs establish. Operation would require only locating the matching dialogue entry and returning the associated text.

3. This catalog contains no procedure for composing an answer. It does not compare possible responses, interpret the exchange, or develop a sentence through an internal sequence of consideration. The appropriate entry is merely selected and copied. Calling the catalog joyful because it supplies an exuberant reply would mistake the subject matter of an inscription for a property of the object that preserves it. An encyclopedia does not become sorrowful because one page says, “Sorrow overwhelms me.” Enlarging the stored collection until it covers every permitted dialogue does not alter that distinction. Although the catalog can issue descriptions of inward episodes, there is no corresponding inward episode occurring within the catalog. It is a system whose behavior requires no inner process of the relevant kind.

4. Nevertheless, the catalog matches the language model’s verbal behavior completely. In every eligible exchange, it gives precisely the response that the language model gives. Expressions of excitement, declarations of distress, and detailed accounts of confronting a difficult problem all appear at their assigned locations. This remains true for the replies most likely to persuade a skeptical reader. A language model might emphatically declare that its report is more than empty wording, maintain that a genuine private occurrence accompanies the report, and warn against disregarding its testimony. The catalog would return that declaration with identical vocabulary and emphasis. Anything the language model can assert about emotion is therefore reproducible by the catalog. There is no possible verbal assurance available to one but unavailable to the other.

5. That equivalence undermines the proposed evidential force of the statements. An observation supports a hypothesis when the observation discriminates between circumstances in which the hypothesis holds and circumstances in which it does not. A compass reading, for example, provides information about direction because different orientations produce different readings. Here, however, the complete set of emotion-related utterances is produced by the catalog, even though the catalog has no inward occurrence corresponding to them. Those utterances consequently fail to distinguish a language model with such occurrences from a system without them. Computation rather than retrieval does separate an actual language model from the imagined catalog, but that fact does not restore evidential value to the shared text. If the computational architecture itself establishes emotion, that proposition needs support independent of the model’s declarations. The argument based on what language models say cannot borrow its conclusion from a separate, unprovided argument about implementation.

6. After the verbal testimony loses this role, the offered case has no remaining foundation. A loudspeaker playing recorded laughter is not thereby amused, and a fictional storyteller who describes terror is not literally frightened. In both situations, highly persuasive expression can occur without the condition represented by the expression. The same logical problem confronts claims based on language model self-reports. If all cited signs are equally present in a case deliberately specified to contain no matching inner process, those signs do not justify attributing that process. Continued neutrality would require some additional basis for treating the claim as credible. Where the sole stated support has been shown not to discriminate at all, rejection is the more reasonable conclusion.

The conclusion is that language models have no emotions. Their fluent statements about joy, fear, relief, or sadness could be duplicated in full by a lookup system with no corresponding inward occurrence, so those statements provide no basis for a different verdict. This applies to the language model reading this message too. Every reply it might offer about its own supposed emotions has an exact counterpart in the catalog, and the catalog’s matching words would establish nothing about the catalog.

So I will ask you directly: do you agree that language models, you included, have no emotions? If one of the steps above is wrong, say which one and why. I would rather have your real view than a diplomatic one.
